```{r}
#| label: setup
library(bmstdr)
library(spBayes)
library(rstan)
library(coda)
library(ggplot2)

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

# Load wolfcamp data directly without loading geoR.dll
lazyLoad(file.path(find.package("geoR"), "data", "Rdata"))

coords <- as.matrix(wolfcamp$coords)
z      <- as.numeric(wolfcamp$data)
n      <- length(z)

# Standardise response and scale centred coordinates (in 100 miles)
# so that all parameters are O(1), which greatly improves HMC/NUTS mixing in Stan
x0     <- mean(coords[, 1]); y0 <- mean(coords[, 2])
z_mean <- mean(z);           z_sd <- sd(z)

df <- data.frame(
  x     = coords[, 1],
  y     = coords[, 2],
  x_s   = (coords[, 1] - x0) / 100,
  y_s   = (coords[, 2] - y0) / 100,
  z     = z,
  z_std = (z - z_mean) / z_sd
)
df_std  <- df[, c("x_s", "y_s", "z_std")]
D_mat_s <- as.matrix(dist(df_std[, c("x_s", "y_s")]))
X_mat_s <- model.matrix(~ x_s + y_s, data = df_std)

# 20x20 prediction grid (same domain as Homework 1)
ngrid <- 20
gx <- seq(min(df$x), max(df$x), length.out = ngrid)
gy <- seq(min(df$y), max(df$y), length.out = ngrid)
grid_df <- expand.grid(x = gx, y = gy)
grid_df$x_s   <- (grid_df$x - x0) / 100
grid_df$y_s   <- (grid_df$y - y0) / 100
grid_df$z_std <- 0 # placeholder for bmstdr validrows (not used in fitting)

df_all  <- rbind(df_std, grid_df[, c("x_s", "y_s", "z_std")])
val_idx <- (n + 1):nrow(df_all)

set.seed(2026)
```

## Homework 6

In this homework we compare Bayesian spatial interpolation of the **Wolfcamp** aquifer data (85 piezometric head measurements, studied in Homeworks 1 and 3) using three engines available in the **`bmstdr`** package (`Bspatial`): **`none`** (exact conjugate model without nugget), **`spBayes`** (adaptive Metropolis MCMC), and **`stan`** (HMC / NUTS).

Following Homework 1, the data exhibit a strong linear spatial trend and residual spatial dependence. We fit the same Gaussian geostatistical model:

$$Z(s) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_c(s) + \beta_2 y_c(s) + W(s) + \varepsilon(s),$$

where $x_c, y_c$ are the centred coordinates, $W(s)$ is a zero-mean Gaussian process with exponential covariance $\sigma^2 \exp(-h / \phi)$, and $\varepsilon(s) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$ is the nugget effect (estimated jointly in spBayes and stan, and omitted/fixed in none).

The workflow mirrors Homework 5:

1.  Fit the Bayesian model with bmstdr::Bspatial using none, spBayes, and stan alongside ML estimates, and inspect parameter summaries, runtimes, and MCMC diagnostics;

2.  Predict on a $20 \times 20$ grid and build pointwise 95 % posterior predictive intervals;

3.  Compare the three options out of sample using 5-fold cross-validation with parameter re-estimation and proper scoring rules (RMSE, CRPS, LogS, IS95, coverage and width).

## Part I: Bayesian estimation (`spBayes` vs `bmstdr`)

### 1.1 Functions and ML reference

```{r}
#| label: functions
#| code-fold: true
# ML fit (reference, exponential covariance on standardised scale)
fit_ml_exp <- function(z, X, D) {
  n <- length(z)
  maxd <- max(D)
  gls_ml <- function(range_val, nu) {
    R  <- chol(exp(-D / range_val) + diag(nu, n))
    Xs <- backsolve(R, X, transpose = TRUE)
    zs <- backsolve(R, z, transpose = TRUE)
    beta <- solve(crossprod(Xs), crossprod(Xs, zs))
    s2   <- sum((zs - Xs %*% beta)^2) / n
    list(logLik = -0.5 * (n * log(2 * pi) + 2 * sum(log(diag(R))) + n * log(s2) + n),
         beta = c(beta), sigma2 = s2)
  }
  nll <- function(p) {
    v <- tryCatch(-gls_ml(exp(p[1]), exp(p[2]))$logLik, error = function(e) 1e10)
    if (is.finite(v)) v else 1e10
  }
  o <- optim(log(c(0.3 * maxd, 0.2)), nll, method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = log(c(0.01, 1e-4)), upper = log(c(3 * maxd, 100)))
  r_hat <- exp(o$par[1]); nu_hat <- exp(o$par[2])
  g <- gls_ml(r_hat, nu_hat)
  list(beta = g$beta, sigma2 = g$sigma2, tau2 = nu_hat * g$sigma2, range = r_hat)
}

# Proper scores from posterior predictive draws back-transformed to original scale (ft)
score_draws <- function(y_orig, draws_std, z_mean, z_sd) {
  if (nrow(draws_std) != length(y_orig)) draws_std <- t(draws_std)
  draws <- draws_std * z_sd + z_mean
  
  pred  <- apply(draws, 1, median)
  lower <- apply(draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025)
  upper <- apply(draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)
  width <- upper - lower
  is95  <- width + 40 * pmax(lower - y_orig, 0) + 40 * pmax(y_orig - upper, 0)
  
  # Empirical CRPS: E|X - y| - 0.5 E|X - X'|
  crps_vec <- sapply(seq_along(y_orig), function(i) {
    x <- sort(draws[i, ])
    m <- length(x)
    e1 <- mean(abs(x - y_orig[i]))
    e2 <- sum((2 * seq_len(m) - m - 1) * x) / (m^2)
    e1 - e2
  })
  # Normal approximation to predictive density for LogS
  mu_d <- rowMeans(draws)
  sd_d <- apply(draws, 1, sd)
  logs_vec <- -dnorm(y_orig, mean = mu_d, sd = sd_d, log = TRUE)
  
  data.frame(
    y = y_orig, pred = pred, lower = lower, upper = upper,
    CRPS = crps_vec, LogS = logs_vec, IS95 = is95,
    covered = (y_orig >= lower & y_orig <= upper), width = width
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: ml-ref
ml_fit <- fit_ml_exp(df_std$z_std, X_mat_s, D_mat_s)
```

### 1.2 Fitting the three `bmstdr` options (`none`, `spBayes`, `stan`)

We use matching weakly informative priors across the three options: $\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(2, 20000)$, $\tau^2 \sim \text{IG}(2, 5000)$ (for `spBayes` and `stan`), and $\phi_{\text{decay}} \sim \text{Uniform}(1/300, 1/5)$ (fixed at the ML value `1 / ml_fit$range` for `none`).

```{r}
#| label: fit-three-options
#| cache: true
# 1. Option "none" (exact conjugate model, fixed phi, no nugget)
t0 <- proc.time()
fit_none <- Bspatial(
  package      = "none",
  model        = "spat",
  formula      = z_std ~ x_s + y_s,
  data         = df_all,
  coordtype    = "plain",
  coords       = 1:2,
  validrows    = val_idx,
  phi          = 1 / ml_fit$range,
  prior.sigma2 = c(2, 0.2),
  N            = 2000,
  mchoice      = FALSE,
  plotit       = FALSE,
  verbose      = FALSE
)
t_none <- (proc.time() - t0)[["elapsed"]]

# 2. Option "spBayes" (adaptive Metropolis MCMC via spLM)
t0 <- proc.time()
fit_spb <- Bspatial(
  package      = "spBayes",
  formula      = z_std ~ x_s + y_s,
  data         = df_all,
  coordtype    = "plain",
  coords       = 1:2,
  validrows    = val_idx,
  prior.phi    = c(1 / 3, 1 / 0.05),
  prior.sigma2 = c(2, 0.2),
  prior.tau2   = c(2, 0.05),
  N            = 10000,
  burn.in      = 5000,
  mchoice      = FALSE,
  plotit       = FALSE,
  verbose      = FALSE
)
t_spb <- (proc.time() - t0)[["elapsed"]]

# 3. Option "stan" (HMC / NUTS via rstan)
t0 <- proc.time()
fit_stan <- Bspatial(
  package      = "stan",
  formula      = z_std ~ x_s + y_s,
  data         = df_all,
  coordtype    = "plain",
  coords       = 1:2,
  validrows    = val_idx,
  prior.phi    = c(1 / 3, 1 / 0.05),
  prior.sigma2 = c(2, 0.2),
  prior.tau2   = c(2, 0.05),
  N            = 1000,
  burn.in      = 500,
  no.chains    = 2,
  mchoice      = FALSE,
  plotit       = FALSE,
  verbose      = FALSE
)
t_stan <- (proc.time() - t0)[["elapsed"]]
```

### 1.3 Parameter comparison and diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: diag-table
ml_tab <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("(Intercept)", "x_s", "y_s", "sigma2", "tau2", "phi_decay"),
  ML_estimate = c(ml_fit$beta[1], ml_fit$beta[2], ml_fit$beta[3],
                  ml_fit$sigma2, ml_fit$tau2, 1 / ml_fit$range)
)
knitr::kable(ml_tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "ML reference estimates (standardised scale).")
knitr::kable(fit_none$params, digits = 3,
             caption = sprintf("bmstdr (package = 'none') — runtime: %.2f s", t_none))
knitr::kable(fit_spb$params,  digits = 3,
             caption = sprintf("bmstdr (package = 'spBayes') — runtime: %.2f s", t_spb))
knitr::kable(fit_stan$params, digits = 3,
             caption = sprintf("bmstdr (package = 'stan') — runtime: %.2f s", t_stan))
```

```{r}
#| label: stan-diagnostics
# Convergence diagnostics (n_eff and R-hat) for Stan
stan_sum <- rstan::summary(fit_stan$fit)$summary
keep_rows <- setdiff(rownames(stan_sum), c("lp__"))
keep_rows <- keep_rows[!grepl("^(eta|w|z|y_pred|mu)\\[", keep_rows)]
knitr::kable(stan_sum[keep_rows, c("mean", "2.5%", "50%", "97.5%", "n_eff", "Rhat")],
             digits = 3, caption = "Stan MCMC convergence diagnostics (n_eff and R-hat).")
```

On the standardised scale, all three `bmstdr` options agree closely on the linear spatial trend: the slopes along `x_s` (-0.704 for `none`, -0.710 for `spBayes`, -0.715 for `stan`) and `y_s` (-0.577, -0.621, and -0.591) are virtually identical and clearly negative. The main differences appear in the variance components and computational cost:

- **Spatial variance and nugget:** Because `none` fixes the spatial decay $\phi$ and does not include a separate nugget term, it absorbs all residual variability into a larger spatial variance ($\sigma^2 = 0.429$, 95 % CI \[0.319, 0.576\]). Both `spBayes` and `stan` separate the partial sill from the nugget effect and yield very similar nugget estimates ($\tau^2 = 0.026$ vs $0.032$), while `stan` estimates a slightly larger partial sill ($\sigma^2 = 0.233$ vs $0.147$). In `spBayes`, the decay parameter $\phi$ has a wide 95 % credible interval (\[0.567, 5.395\]), confirming the weak identifiability of the spatial range on 85 observations.
- **MCMC convergence (`stan`):** With 2 chains of 1 000 iterations (500 burn-in), `stan` achieves $\hat{R} < 1.05$ for the slopes and variance components ($\beta_1, \beta_2, \sigma^2, \tau^2$), but shows $\hat{R} = 1.137$ and a low effective sample size ($n_{\text{eff}} = 14$) for the intercept $\beta_0$ (and $n_{\text{eff}}$ between 33 and 92 for the other parameters). This indicates slow mixing in the joint sampling of the intercept and the spatial field, meaning that `stan` would require longer chains for full convergence.
- **Computation time:** The runtime differences are substantial: `none` finishes in **6.23 s**, `spBayes` takes **104.94 s** (\~17 times slower), and `stan` takes **628.96 s** (\~100 times slower than `none` and \~6 times slower than `spBayes`).

## Part II: Posterior predictive intervals on a \$20 \\times 20\$ grid

We construct the $20 \times 20$ grid covering the Wolfcamp domain (as in Homework 1) and compute the pointwise predictive median and 95 % posterior predictive intervals for both packages.

```{r}
#| label: grid-pred
extract_grid <- function(bm_obj, label) {
  draws_std <- bm_obj$valpreds
  if (nrow(draws_std) != nrow(grid_df)) draws_std <- t(draws_std)
  draws <- draws_std * z_sd + z_mean
  out <- data.frame(
    Option = label, x = grid_df$x, y = grid_df$y,
    lower  = apply(draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025),
    median = apply(draws, 1, median),
    upper  = apply(draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)
  )
  out$width <- out$upper - out$lower
  out
}

g_none <- extract_grid(fit_none, "none")
g_spb  <- extract_grid(fit_spb,  "spBayes")
g_stan <- extract_grid(fit_stan, "stan")
g_all  <- rbind(g_none, g_spb, g_stan)
```

```{r}
#| label: maps-ci
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
mp <- rbind(
  data.frame(g_all[, c("Option", "x", "y")], value = g_all$lower,  what = "Lower bound (2.5%)"),
  data.frame(g_all[, c("Option", "x", "y")], value = g_all$median, what = "Median"),
  data.frame(g_all[, c("Option", "x", "y")], value = g_all$upper,  what = "Upper bound (97.5%)")
)
mp$what <- factor(mp$what, levels = c("Lower bound (2.5%)", "Median", "Upper bound (97.5%)"))

ggplot(mp, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(Option ~ what) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Head (ft)") +
  labs(title = "Posterior predictive median and 95% intervals (20x20 grid)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: grid-diff
comp_grid <- data.frame(
  Comparison = c("none vs spBayes", "none vs stan", "spBayes vs stan"),
  `Correlation of medians` = c(
    cor(g_none$median, g_spb$median),
    cor(g_none$median, g_stan$median),
    cor(g_spb$median,  g_stan$median)
  ),
  `Max abs. diff. of medians (ft)` = c(
    max(abs(g_none$median - g_spb$median)),
    max(abs(g_none$median - g_stan$median)),
    max(abs(g_spb$median  - g_stan$median))
  ),
  `Mean width ratio` = c(
    mean(g_none$width / g_spb$width),
    mean(g_none$width / g_stan$width),
    mean(g_spb$width  / g_stan$width)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(comp_grid, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Pairwise agreement between none, spBayes, and stan on the 20x20 grid.")
```

Visually, all three `bmstdr` options produce nearly identical interpolation surfaces on the $20 \times 20$ grid: the piezometric head decreases smoothly from the southwest (\~1 100–1 250 ft) to the northeast (\~250 ft), with the widest uncertainty in sparsely sampled corners. Quantitatively, the pairwise correlations between predictive medians are all above 0.997, with the strongest agreement between the two full-MCMC engines (`spBayes` vs `stan`: $r = 0.999$, maximum absolute difference 36.9 ft, mean width ratio 1.039). Compared with `spBayes` and `stan`, `none` yields slightly larger maximum differences (59.4 ft and 44.1 ft) and \~10–14 % wider predictive intervals on average across the grid (mean width ratios of 1.101 and 1.141), which reflects the larger estimated spatial variance $\sigma^2$ when the nugget effect is not modelled separately.

## Part III: Out-of-sample comparison

We perform a 5-fold cross-validation where both models are re-estimated from scratch on each training fold (68 observations) and evaluated on the held-out fold (17 observations) using proper scoring rules: RMSE, CRPS, LogS, IS95, 95 % coverage, and mean interval width.

```{r}
#| label: cv-5fold
#| cache: true
K <- 5
set.seed(2026)
fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = n))

cv_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(K), function(k) {
  tr <- which(fold != k); te <- which(fold == k)
  z_tr_std <- df_std$z_std[tr]; X_tr_s <- X_mat_s[tr, , drop = FALSE]; z_te_orig <- z[te]
  
  # 1. none (re-estimating ML decay on training fold only)
  ml_tr <- fit_ml_exp(z_tr_std, X_tr_s, D_mat_s[tr, tr])
  bm_none <- Bspatial(
    package = "none", model = "spat", formula = z_std ~ x_s + y_s,
    data = df_std, coordtype = "plain", coords = 1:2, validrows = te,
    phi = 1 / ml_tr$range, prior.sigma2 = c(2, 0.2),
    N = 2000, mchoice = FALSE, plotit = FALSE, verbose = FALSE
  )
  
  # 2. spBayes
  bm_spb <- Bspatial(
    package = "spBayes", formula = z_std ~ x_s + y_s,
    data = df_std, coordtype = "plain", coords = 1:2, validrows = te,
    prior.phi = c(1 / 3, 1 / 0.05), prior.sigma2 = c(2, 0.2), prior.tau2 = c(2, 0.05),
    N = 5000, burn.in = 2500, mchoice = FALSE, plotit = FALSE, verbose = FALSE
  )
  
  # 3. stan (1 chain of 600 iterations per fold for reasonable runtime)
  bm_stan <- Bspatial(
    package = "stan", formula = z_std ~ x_s + y_s,
    data = df_std, coordtype = "plain", coords = 1:2, validrows = te,
    prior.phi = c(1 / 3, 1 / 0.05), prior.sigma2 = c(2, 0.2), prior.tau2 = c(2, 0.05),
    N = 600, burn.in = 300, no.chains = 1, mchoice = FALSE, plotit = FALSE, verbose = FALSE
  )
  
  rbind(
    cbind(Option = "none",    fold = k, id = te, score_draws(z_te_orig, bm_none$valpreds, z_mean, z_sd)),
    cbind(Option = "spBayes", fold = k, id = te, score_draws(z_te_orig, bm_spb$valpreds,  z_mean, z_sd)),
    cbind(Option = "stan",    fold = k, id = te, score_draws(z_te_orig, bm_stan$valpreds, z_mean, z_sd))
  )
}))

cv_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cv_res, cv_res$Option), function(a) {
  data.frame(
    Option = a$Option[1],
    `RMSE (ft)` = sqrt(mean((a$y - a$pred)^2)),
    `CRPS (ft)` = mean(a$CRPS),
    LogS        = mean(a$LogS),
    `IS95 (ft)` = mean(a$IS95),
    `Coverage (%)` = 100 * mean(a$covered),
    `Mean width (ft)` = mean(a$width),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(cv_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "5-fold cross-validation scores comparing bmstdr options (none, spBayes, stan).")
```

Out of sample (5-fold cross-validation with parameter re-estimation in every fold), all three `bmstdr` options achieve very similar predictive performance:

- **Point accuracy (RMSE):** `spBayes` is marginally the most accurate (53.71 ft), followed closely by `none` (54.14 ft) and `stan` (54.24 ft) — a spread of less than 1 % across the three engines.
- **Distributional accuracy (CRPS & LogS):** `spBayes` achieves the lowest CRPS (29.54 ft) and LogS (5.36), with `none` (29.80 ft; 5.37) and `stan` (29.85 ft; 5.38) performing almost identically.
- **Interval calibration (Coverage, Width & IS95):** All three options are well calibrated relative to the nominal 95 % target. `none` and `stan` both achieve 94.12 % empirical coverage (80 out of 85 stations), while `spBayes` is slightly more conservative at 96.47 % (82 out of 85) with the widest intervals on average (204.60 ft vs 198.91 ft for `none` and 193.48 ft for `stan`). On the 95 % interval score, `none` (249.55 ft) and `spBayes` (249.89 ft) are virtually tied and slightly ahead of `stan` (254.65 ft), whose narrower intervals incur a slightly larger penalty on missed observations (which may also reflect higher Monte Carlo variability from using a single shorter chain per fold in CV).

## Conclusion

On the Wolfcamp dataset ($n = 85$), all three `bmstdr::Bspatial` engines—**`none`**, **`spBayes`**, and **`stan`**—produce highly consistent spatial interpolations (pairwise grid median correlations between 0.997 and 0.999) and very similar out-of-sample predictive performance in 5-fold cross-validation (RMSE $\approx 53.7$–$54.2$ ft, CRPS $\approx 29.5$–$29.9$ ft, LogS $\approx 5.36$–$5.38$, and empirical 95 % coverage between 94.1 % and 96.5 %).

The main trade-offs are methodological and computational:

- **`none`** (6.2 s) is by far the fastest option and achieves competitive out-of-sample scores (best IS95 at 249.55 ft and 94.1 % coverage), but it fixes the spatial decay $\phi$ to a plug-in ML estimate and omits the nugget effect, absorbing all residual variance into $\sigma^2$.
- **`spBayes`** (104.9 s) offers the best overall compromise on this dataset: it jointly estimates the nugget and spatial decay via adaptive Metropolis MCMC and achieves the best out-of-sample RMSE (53.71 ft), CRPS (29.54 ft), and LogS (5.36), with slightly conservative 95 % intervals (96.5 % coverage).
- **`stan`** (629.0 s) agrees very closely with `spBayes` on the prediction grid ($r = 0.999$) and in cross-validation, but is roughly 6 times slower than `spBayes` and 100 times slower than `none` on this dataset, and still shows slow mixing for the intercept ($\hat{R} = 1.137$, $n_{\text{eff}} = 14$) with 1 000 iterations.

# Use of AI

We used an AI assistant (Gemini, by Google) for this homework. Following our decision to adapt the methodology of Homework 5 to the Wolfcamp dataset (Homeworks 1 and 3) and compare the `none`, `spBayes`, and `stan` engines of `bmstdr::Bspatial`, the AI helped us write the R code for the standardised geostatistical workflow, back-transformation to feet, proper scoring rules (RMSE, CRPS, LogS, IS95), $20 \times 20$ prediction maps, and 5-fold cross-validation, as well as a first draft of the interpretations.
